name: Oscar Wilde
bio: Dublin-born writer; born 16 October 1854 at 21 Westland Row, educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford. Married Constance Lloyd on 29 May 1884; two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Convicted 25 May 1895 and sentenced to two years' hard labour following the three trials of that spring; released 19 May 1897 and lived thereafter in France and Italy. Died 30 November 1900 at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, of cerebral meningitis; buried at Bagneux, moved to Père Lachaise in 1909.
bio_note: All facts from the Chronological Table, Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), pp. viii-xii (repo PDF 8-12), read as page images 2026-08-03.

context_engagements.note: Not a person-to-person engagement. Recorded because Wilde, two years out from the trials, states in a private letter that he knows he has become a case in the medical literature of homosexuality - and objects to the arithmetic of it rather than the diagnosis.

sources.quote: My life cannot be patched up. There is a doom on it. Neither to myself, nor others, am I any longer a joy. I am now simply an ordinary pauper of a rather low order: the fact that I am also a pathological problem in the eyes of German scientists is only interesting to German scientists: and even in their works I am tabulated, and come under the law of averages! Quantum mutatus!
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Saturday [11 December 1897], Villa Giudice, Posilippo (MS Hyde). 'averages' is italicised in the printed text; the Latin is Virgil, 'How changed from what he once was'. THE GERMAN SCIENTISTS are the sexologists - Krafft-Ebing's Psychopathia Sexualis and its successors, in which the Wilde trials had become standard case material within two years. Wilde is describing his own conversion into a data point, and the sting he picks out is not being called pathological but being TABULATED: made ordinary, averaged, one of a class. No specific work is named on the page and none is inferred here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own awareness that he had become a case study in the medical literature of homosexuality, in his lifetime.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1054; printed folio 1006 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

roster_note: The collective 'unnamed and one-scene companions' entry was removed 2026-08-04: every named man in it now has his own node and edge (Andre, Pietro, le petit Georges, the Napoule fisherman, the Cafe d'Egypte Egyptian, Raphael, Fortune, the Naples 'Sea-God'), so the entry only duplicated them. TWO THINGS IT CARRIED HAVE NO NODE: (1) the unnamed 'beautiful boy in grey velvet' seen with Wilde outside a cafe behind the Madeleine by Aleck Ross, late March 1900 (Complete Letters printed 1177) - a roster candidate on exactly the same footing as the Sea-God and the Napoule fisherman, who are already nodes; and (2) Wilde's general remark on the Riviera fishing population, 27 December 1898 (printed 1112), which is a remark rather than a person.
